# Linked Lists in C

A **linked list** is a chain: each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node, and the last points at nothing (**NULL**). To get anywhere you start at **head** and follow the arrows. Inserting or removing is just re-pointing an arrow or two, with no shuffling of everything after it.

The catch is that the arrows are the only thing holding the list together. Re-point one in the wrong order and everything after it is gone: no error, no crash, the nodes are simply unreachable.

Here the nodes live in a **pool**: two arrays, `val[]` and `nxt[]`, where a "pointer" is just a slot number and -1 means NULL. That's how lists are built in kernels, games and embedded code, and it can't crash with a bad address.

The question: **why does the order of three lines in the reverse matter so much?**

How the cells run:

- **C runs in your browser.** xcc compiles the cell to WebAssembly on the page, so it runs at once, on the website too. It reads the dropdown with `#include <nb.h>` and records every pointer change in a `__NB_SET__` line.
- **The player is an HTML cell**; **JavaScript** counts the nodes reachable at every step.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 2. Build and change the list in C

> In C, build a singly linked list in a node pool (arrays val and nxt of 32 slots, an index as the pointer and -1 as NULL, no malloc) with push_back, insert_after, remove and an in-place reverse. Read nb.ll_reverse with <nb.h>: careful reverses by remembering next, flipping the arrow and stepping on; flip_first flips the arrow before remembering next. Push 10, 20, 30 and 40, insert 25 after 20, remove 30 and reverse. Record a frame after every pointer move or change, with the operation, head, both arrays, the variables prev, cur and next (-2 when unused) and a sentence saying what happened, and publish nb.ll = {mode, frames} with a `__NB_SET__` line. Print the list after each operation.

- **`insert_after`** sets the new node's arrow *first*, then points the target at the new node. The other way round, the target would forget the rest of the list before anyone copied it.
- **`reverse_list`** does three things per node: remember `next`, flip the arrow to point back at `prev`, step on. The careless version flips first, so when it then reads "next" it gets the node it just pointed back at.
- **`frame()`** prints the whole state after every change, so the player and the JS cell see exactly what the program did.

## 4. Count what is reachable

> In JavaScript, follow the arrows in every frame of nb.ll and count the nodes the program can still reach: from head, or from the variables prev, cur and next, stopping if it loops. Print the list read from head at the end of each operation, how many nodes are lost at the end, and whether the final list is the original one reversed (40, 25, 20, 10). Return a Vega-Lite line chart of reachable nodes and nodes in the pool against step, with the points coloured by operation.

A node nobody points at can never be reached again. In C with `malloc` it would also never be freed: a **memory leak**. This cell follows the arrows in every recorded frame, as the program would: from head, and from whatever its variables still hold. Halfway through a careful reverse, head only reaches one node, but `next` holds on to the rest.

## What the run shows

- **Each operation changes one or two arrows.** Inserting 25 sets two (the new node's, then 20's); removing 30 sets one (20's now skips it). Nothing else in the list moves: that's the point of a linked list.
- **The careful reverse never loses a node.** It takes 33 recorded steps in all, and while it runs, the program can always reach all 4 nodes, even when head only reaches one: the nodes it hasn't flipped yet are held by `next`. It ends with 40 → 25 → 20 → 10.
- **The careless reverse loses three nodes in one step.** Flipping 10's arrow before reading where it pointed leaves "next" pointing back at NULL. The loop stops after one node, head is 10, and 20, 25 and 40 can never be reached again; reachable nodes drop from 4 to 1. It doesn't crash or warn: it just returns a list of one.
- **The pool never forgets.** 30, removed on purpose, still sits in slot 2: nothing points at it, so with `malloc` this would be a memory leak unless it were freed.
- **`push_back` walks the whole list** to find the end: to add 40, `cur` visits 10, 20 and 30 before the new node can be linked. A `tail` pointer would make it one step.

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **Predict, then switch.** With *Careless*, how many nodes will still be reachable after the reverse? Then run the C and JS cells.
- **A cheaper end.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Keep a tail index too, so push_back needs no walk."* Count the frames before and after.
- **Reuse the gaps.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Keep a free list of removed slots and reuse them in alloc_node."* The lost slot for 30 comes back.
- **Find the middle.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Find the middle node with a slow pointer that moves one step and a fast one that moves two, recording frames."*
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the C cell and ask why `insert_after` must set the new node's arrow first.
